To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

invertases are key regulators of plant compensatory growth following damage, and that the ability to up-regulate invertase expression is a genetic component underlying the phenomenon of over-compensation.

1) the invertase gene INV2 is up-regulated in the Columbia-4 genotype, and that INV2 is essential for overcompensation, 2) the invertase genes INV1 and INV2 are up-regulated in Columbia-4 and are essential for overcompensatory fruit production, and 3) the invertase INV3 is down-regulated in the Landsberg erecta genotype and its knock-out mutant exhibits undercompensation for fitness following damage.
invertase genes are up-regulated in the overcompensating genotype, and that knockout mutants of two invertases exhibit undercompensation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification and characterization of the specific genes and molecular pathways that are responsible for the phenomenon of over-compensation in plants, which is a key component in the evolution of plant-herbivore interactions.
identifying genes that are involved in a plant’s ability to overcome damage, a trait that is likely to be under strong natural selection.
the role of invertase genes and the OPPP pathway in the phenomenon of plant compensation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results indicate that invertases play an important role in the phenomenon of plant overcompensation.
our data indicate that invertases play a critical role in plant compensatory growth and fitness, and thus are likely to be a target of natural selection for plants growing in the wild.
invertases, and the OPPP, are essential for normal plant development, and that these enzymes are key components in plants’ abilities to compensate for apical damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plants that overcompensate for fitness following simulated herbivory have the ability to upregulate a large set of invertase genes that are not upregulated in plants that undercompensate.
the ability to overcompensate is a complex phenomenon that is likely regulated by multiple pathways and genes, and that invertases are one of the key players.
invertases, and specifically the invertase gene At4g34230 and At5g54140 (which were up-regulated by Col-4 but down-regulated by Ler) play a key role in the phenomenon of over-compensation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability to overcompensate for fitness following damage is not a fixed characteristic, but rather a dynamic one that can be manipulated by genetic engineering.
the ability to compensate for damage is a highly complex phenomenon, involving a suite of genes and pathways, and that the genetic basis of this phenomenon is not the same across all plant species.
the ability of plants to overcompensate is a highly plastic trait and that a suite of genes, including invertases, contribute to this plasticity.
